rows.claim: Others distinguish inner dimensions: huwa is Essence beyond attributes, while Allah is Essence with the totality of attributes, not a difference in divinity.
rows.anchor: huwa indicates the Essence qua Essence beyond consideration of Its Attributes, and Allāh indicates “the Essence with the totality of the Attributes”

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī says Allah gathers positive attributes and aḥad negative attributes; together they give a complete understanding, and Allah is the “Gathering Name.”
rows.anchor: Allāh can also be seen as conveying the totality of positive Divine Attributes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṣamad, used only here in the Qur'an and only of God, lexically means solid, impenetrable, or not hollow.
rows.anchor: nontheological meaning indicates something solid and impenetrable or simply“not hollow”

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some understand al-Ṣamad as something beyond all comprehension.
rows.anchor: some take al-Ṣamad to indicate something that is beyond all comprehension

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Theologically, some read al-Ṣamad as the first cause: an eternally self-sufficient being who remains after creation ceases.
rows.anchor: al-Ṣamad is interpreted by some as an allusion to the Primary or Initial Cause of all things

rows.speaker: al-Zamakhsharī
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī parses al-Ṣamad as the sought-to Master: creation seeks Him for every need and depends on Him, while He needs none.
rows.anchor: According to al-Zamakhsharī, in this context, “Al-Ṣamad is a verb taking the meaning of the passive participle

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The many explanations converge on God as Master and ontological source, with all things dependent on Him and He independent of all.
rows.anchor: most of which are different formulations confirming that God is the Master and ontological Source of all things

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some read this verse as two separate verses.
rows.anchor: This verse was read by some as two verses

rows.speaker: vast majority of Muslims
rows.claim: The verse categorically denies every form of divine progeny, repudiating all such claims.
rows.anchor: It denies categorically any form of Divine progeny and is thus seen by the vast majority of Muslims

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although read as denying Jesus is God's Son, the verse's strongest context is pagan Arab claims; links to Christianity are somewhat tenuous.
rows.anchor: Attempts to link this verse to discussions of Christianity are thus somewhat tenuous

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is best understood through the reported occasions of revelation and the Qur'an's critique of pagan claims that God had daughters or other offspring.
rows.anchor: it is best understood in relation to the possible occasions of revelation mentioned in the sūrah introduction

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Christian “Son of God” means the pretemporal, uncreated Word begotten before time; pagan Arab divine offspring implied temporal, physical progeny.
rows.anchor: For Christianity, the term “Son of God” refers to Jesus as the pretemporal, uncreated Word of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse reinforces oneness by affirming God's uniqueness: shared descriptors such as living, seeing, and hearing do not make anything equal or like His Essence.
rows.anchor: nothing bears any likeness or equality with God’s Essence or Self

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nothing exists independently of God: He is transcendent in Essence, yet immanent in worldly manifestation and present wherever one turns.
rows.anchor: With regard to the Divine Essence, God is absolutely transcendent

rows.speaker: Mujāhid
rows.claim: Mujāhid interprets the verse to mean God has no spouse.
rows.anchor: According to Mujāhid, this verse means that God does not have a spouse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse also refutes pre-Islamic Arabs who attributed kinship between God and jinn.
rows.anchor: It is also taken as a refutation of the pre-Islamic Arabs, who had ascribed jinn as partners to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most date al-Falaq and al-Nās to the Makkan period; some say Madinan, while others suspend judgment for lack of conclusive evidence.
rows.anchor: revealed during the Makkan period, although some believe that

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Falaq takes its name from daybreak, which the Prophet is told to swear by in verse 1.
rows.anchor: Al-Falaq takes its name from the daybreak, by which the Prophet is told to swear in the first verse

rows.speaker: many
rows.claim: Many who consider the surahs Makkan connect them to an illness caused by a sorceress's spell; Gabriel located her knotted string, and ʿAlī retrieved it so the Prophet could recite fourteen verses to undo fourteen knots.
rows.anchor: the Prophet was stricken with an illness as a result of a spell put upon him by a sorceress

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Falaq and al-Nās are “The Two Protectors,” still used for protection from evils including the evil eye and spells.
rows.anchor: and are used by Muslims to this day for

rows.speaker: Ubayy ibn Kaʿb
rows.claim: Early Companions debated whether the two surahs were Qur'an or a special supplication; Ubayy reports the Messenger confirmed they were revealed to and recited by him as Qur'an, rejecting Ibn Masʿūd's contrary view.
rows.anchor: Ubayy said, ‘I asked God’s Messenger about them, and he said, “They have been revealed to me

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Falaq means dawn light or rising dawn; its root means “cleave,” describing night as cleaved from day.
rows.anchor: Daybreak translates falaq, which indicates “the light of dawn” or “the rising dawn”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Metaphorically, falaq can mean truth emerging from uncertainty; God is the source of understanding, so refuge in Him is refuge in truth from falsehood.
rows.anchor: Falaq can also be used metaphorically to indicate “the emergence of truth after uncertainty”

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some take falaq as the name of Hell, a prison in Hell, or a tree or mountain in the Fire.
rows.anchor: Falaq is also taken by some as a name of Hell, a prison in Hell

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: The evil of what God created can mean Satan and his ilk, Hellfire, evil generally, or evil committed by created beings.
rows.anchor: This verse can be understood as a reference to Satan and his ilk or to Hellfire

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Creation itself can be understood as a veil that both conceals the Creator and reveals His qualities and attributes.
rows.anchor: It can also be understood as a reference to creation itself, which acts as a veil

rows.speaker: most
rows.claim: Most read the verse as nightfall; some read waqaba as the night's cooling. In either case refuge is sought because evildoers spread mischief at night.
rows.anchor: Most interpret this verse as a reference to the darkening of the night, but some take the verb waqaba

rows.claim: Naffathāt specifically describes knot-tying with whispered incantations, but can include everyone practicing black magic.
rows.anchor: engaged in the practice of tying knots in a string and whispering incantations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though grammatically feminine plural, naffathāt need not mean women only; it may mean humans generally, with the spell-working women as a specific example of evil.
rows.anchor: Though the noun is in the feminine plural, it is not necessarily limited to women
